messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi, a 48-year-old Māori man who worked as a roofer, came to treatment after months of feeling as though his life had narrowed around a single assault that he had never been able to put fully into the past. The event had happened after work, when he had been drinking with men he thought were mates; he remembered the smell of alcohol on one of them, the blur of a motorcycle pulling up outside, and then the humiliation and violation of being sexually assaulted when he was too stunned to fight effectively. Since then, he had found that ordinary news reports about assaults or violence could catch him off guard and leave him abruptly tense, as if the story on the radio were not a story at all but a doorway back into that night. The same happened with the hard mechanical whine of a motorcycle outside his home or down on the street near the building sites where he worked. Those sounds had become potent because they seemed to arrive with the force of the original moment, and the smell of alcohol could do the same, bringing back the assault with a blunt immediacy that made him feel exposed and trapped.

What distressed Rangi most was the way his memory of the event did not behave like a normal recollection. He described it as more real and vivid than his memories of ordinary life, as if it sat close to the surface and could be entered without warning. Sometimes, when a trigger hit him, he did not get a clear picture at all but instead felt the full emotional intensity of the assault—shame, fear, and a heavy grief that seemed to come from nowhere—while the scene itself stayed blurred. At other times, a flash of the episode would feel so immediate that he could almost smell the alcohol again and hear the motorcycle in the background. When he remembered what had happened, the grief was overwhelming; he would go quiet, look away, and feel as though he had lost something that could never be recovered, including the easy confidence he had once had in other men and in his own body.

In the months that followed, Rangi began building habits around control, partly because he felt his body had betrayed him and partly because he wanted to avoid anything that might leave him physically stressed and therefore vulnerable. He stopped pushing himself at work when the roof pitch was steep or the weather made the job punishing, and he tried to arrange his day so he would not have to strain too hard. At home, he became strict about eating, telling himself that if he could control what went in, he could at least control something. He also worked hard at keeping busy with other things, filling any empty time with chores, errands, and extra tasks for friends and family. These strategies brought only brief relief. The more tightly he managed himself, the more his body felt like something he had to supervise, and the more likely it seemed that a remembered sensation—a burst of exertion on the roof, the taste or smell of alcohol at a gathering, even a news clip playing in the background—would pull him back into the event. He found that the very effort to stay in control made the assault feel closer, because it kept his attention fixed on how easily he might be overwhelmed.

That same pattern worked in the other direction as well. Because the memories felt so vivid and emotionally charged, Rangi became more determined to avoid situations that reminded him of them. He steered clear of social drinking, declined invitations where alcohol would be present, and altered his routine so he would not have to pass places where motorcycles congregated. At work he preferred jobs that kept him away from particularly taxing physical demands, and he would make excuses if a task seemed likely to leave him winded or sore. Yet the more he avoided strain and the more he filled his days with busyness, the smaller his world became, and the more startling the reminders felt when they did break through. Even a news item on the television in the lunchroom could catch him because he had been trying so hard not to think about what happened. The pattern left him increasingly isolated from his coworkers and more withdrawn with his wife, who noticed that he was always occupied but never at ease.

By the time he sought help, Rangi was exhausted by the constant effort to outrun what kept returning. He was afraid that if he let up on control, even briefly, the memories would flood back with the same force and leave him overwhelmed with grief and shame; at the same time, he was hoping that therapy might help him feel less ruled by those moments when a sound, a smell, or a news report seemed to throw him straight back into the assault.
